Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Condylar growth

The direct pediatric randomized study found no added skeletal or dental benefit at 9 months. Related orthodontic trials and rat studies report mixed findings.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

The direct pediatric randomized study found no added skeletal or dental benefit at 9 months. Related orthodontic trials and rat studies report mixed findings.

Summary of the Evidence

Five exact-category records address the mandible/condyle: one preliminary 14-participant pediatric RCT and four rat experiments. Two related functional-orthodontic RCTs (n=48, n=40) are mapped, not treated as direct condylar-growth studies. No in-vitro/ex-vivo study is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

The direct trial found no added skeletal or dental benefit over twin-block therapy at 9 months. The mapped class II trial reported greater mandibular length and shorter treatment; the class III trial found no significant condylar-position effect and a small volume difference (Amer et al. 2022; Abdulhadi et al., 2022; Khwanda et al., 2022). The direct clinical sample included only 14 children and was preliminary; it cannot exclude small effects or define which growth patterns might respond. The functional-appliance trials are contextual evidence, not direct replications of the condylar-growth intervention.

Primary original study: Amer et al. 2022 mapped clinical report: Aghili et al. 2023

Animal evidence

Four rat studies report greater condylar growth or cartilage/matrix changes, but findings vary: combined treatment did not consistently increase new bone, and LED outperformed laser in one growth comparison (Seifi et al., 2010; El-Bialy et al., 2015; Franco et al., 2019; Eğlenen et al., 2023).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

none identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Amer et al. report 940 nm treatment at 3.9 J/cm² over 16 sessions in 3 months. Aghili et al. used 980 nm at 100 mW, 4 points around the temporomandibular joints for 100 seconds per point, weekly for 3 months. Both are near-infrared, outside the visible band; the clinical contexts differ.

Interpretation

The direct trial is preliminary and cannot rule out a small effect, but it did not demonstrate added benefit. Functional-appliance outcomes are related context rather than evidence for an independent condylar-growth effect. Animal changes in cartilage or bone do not establish clinical improvement in growing children.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow. The small direct pediatric trial found no added benefit, while animal and related trials are mixed.
Publications and records7 unique titles: 5 exact-category and 2 mapped functional-appliance trials.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One small randomized pediatric trial directly evaluates condylar growth and finds no added benefit over functional-appliance treatment. Four rat studies report biological changes, and two mapped orthodontic trials evaluate related mandibular outcomes. The mapped trials are not direct replications of the condylar-growth question, so animal and adjacent clinical findings do not override the direct null result.
